paragraphs: The paper asks whether observed samples are consistent with a specified probability density. It proposes a nonparametric goodness-of-fit test, giving a statistical way to assess agreement between data and a target distribution. The task is to evaluate a proposed distribution, rather than simply fit another model to the observations.

The authors construct a measure of discrepancy using Stein’s method and functions from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. They estimate this discrepancy from samples through a V-statistic involving the kernel and gradients of the target’s log density. This connects the statistical comparison to quantities computed from the observations and the target density.

The test accommodates both independent, identically distributed samples and samples with dependence. A wild bootstrap estimates the reference thresholds used for testing agreement with the target. The paper applies the method to checking approximate Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence, criticizing statistical models, and examining fit against model complexity in nonparametric density estimation. These applications make distribution checking a common tool across several modeling tasks.
icml-2016-a-kernel-test-of-goodness-of-f.tldr: A kernel-based statistical test checks whether independent or dependent samples agree with a target probability density.

paragraphs: This paper connects a convolutional network used for classification with a model that generates images. The derivation assumes a multicategory classifier in which one category comes from a reference distribution. That reference category provides the starting point for constructing a generative random field from the discriminative network.

With the additional assumptions of ReLU nonlinearities and Gaussian white noise as the reference distribution, the resulting model is piecewise Gaussian. Its Gaussian means are specified by an autoencoder. Filters used to encode an image from the bottom up also serve as basis functions for decoding from the top down, while binary activation variables supply the decoding coefficients.

The connection extends to sampling and learning. Langevin sampling is driven by the autoencoder’s reconstruction error, and contrastive divergence learning reconstructs training images through that same autoencoder. The authors also report that maximum likelihood learning can synthesize realistic natural image patterns. The contribution is therefore a conditional theoretical account tying classification, reconstruction, and generation together within one convolutional model.
icml-2016-a-theory-of-generative-convnet.tldr: Under specified classifier, activation, and reference-distribution assumptions, a generative ConvNet links image generation to autoencoder reconstruction.

paragraphs: Multilabel classification predicts a set of labels for each example. The paper focuses on the relationships among those labels, which can contain useful structure even when that structure is unknown beforehand. It argues that deep learning approaches can achieve strong results while still leaving these relationships insufficiently represented.

ADIOS first learns to partition the labels into a structure called a Markov Blanket Chain. It then uses a new deep architecture designed to exploit that partition. The output organization is therefore learned as part of the approach, giving the network a way to use relationships among labels when making its predictions.

Experiments on several popular, large multilabel datasets report significant improvements and benefits for trade-offs specific to multilabel classification. These findings support the usefulness of explicitly organizing the output space in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is the combination of learning label structure and constructing an architecture around it, so that prediction can draw on more than the information used to distinguish each label separately.
icml-2016-adios-architectures-deep-in-ou.tldr: ADIOS learns a structured partition of labels and uses it in a deep architecture to improve multilabel prediction.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization objectives expressed as the ratio of two submodular functions. Its goal is to minimize that ratio, and the authors argue that this formulation arises naturally in real applications. Treating the ratio as its own optimization problem creates a basis for studying both algorithms and the quality of their answers.

The authors connect ratio minimization to related formulations, including minimizing the difference between submodular functions and optimizing with submodular constraints. They develop algorithms with bounded approximation factors. These bounds quantify how closely an algorithm’s answer can approach the optimum, providing a theoretical account of solution quality.

The analysis also establishes a hardness bound, describing a limit on attainable approximation. The strongest proposed algorithm matches that lower bound up to a logarithmic factor, placing its guarantee near the stated theoretical boundary. Empirical evaluations demonstrate performance and good scalability. Together, the theoretical and empirical results address two distinct questions: how good the solutions can be and whether the algorithms remain workable as problems grow.
icml-2016-algorithms-for-optimizing-the-.tldr: The paper develops approximation algorithms for minimizing ratios of submodular functions, with guarantees approaching a hardness bound.

paragraphs: The paper models international interaction records that specify an acting country, an action, a receiving country, and a time. Bayesian Poisson Tucker decomposition uses these linked dimensions to uncover hidden organization in the events. The aim is to represent relationships among countries alongside patterns in what they do and when.

The model discovers country communities and allows a country to belong to multiple communities. It also discovers the number of latent communities. Beyond membership, it learns directed networks of interactions between communities, with different networks associated with action topics and temporal regimes. This lets the representation distinguish who interacts, the kinds of actions involved, and the relevant time patterns.

The authors provide an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo inference algorithm and report better predictive performance than related models. They also find interpretable latent structure that agrees with their knowledge of international relations. These results support both predictive and descriptive uses of the model: forecasting event patterns and organizing observed interactions into understandable communities and relationships.
icml-2016-bayesian-poisson-tucker-decomp.tldr: Bayesian Poisson Tucker decomposition discovers overlapping country communities and interaction patterns across action topics and temporal regimes.

paragraphs: The paper addresses clustering and visualization for data described by many categorical variables. Its approach is to construct topographical features of the underlying distribution, giving these data a geometric interpretation. This representation is intended to reveal how the observations are organized, making distributional structure useful for subsequent analysis.

The proposed algorithm efficiently extracts modes and their attractive basins. Modes represent peaks in the distribution, while attractive basins describe the regions associated with those peaks. Together, these features describe more than isolated representative points: they connect prominent parts of the distribution with the surrounding data regions. The resulting view supports both grouping observations and visualizing their organization.

Experiments on challenging real-world datasets report better clustering performance than state-of-the-art methods. The algorithm also has an embarrassingly parallel structure, meaning its work is particularly amenable to parallel execution. The stated contribution combines a distribution-based way to describe categorical data with an efficient computational method, with the reported experiments supporting its value for clustering.
icml-2016-clustering-high-dimensional-ca.tldr: An efficient, highly parallel algorithm clusters categorical data using distributional peaks and their associated regions.

paragraphs: Nyström approximation makes kernel methods more manageable by constructing a low-rank approximation to a kernel matrix. This paper targets a remaining bottleneck: computing kernel values between each input and every landmark point. With m landmarks and input dimension d, that calculation ordinarily takes time proportional to m times d.

The authors generate structured landmarks using fast transforms, including Haar and Hadamard transforms. Exploiting that structure reduces the stated kernel-evaluation cost to time proportional to m or m log d. The change directly targets a computation that dominates both training and prediction, so it can benefit more than the initial construction of the approximation.

On the webspam dataset, containing over 300,000 points, the proposed method enables kernel SVM prediction with 98% accuracy. Its reported prediction time is 1,000 times faster than LIBSVM and ten times slower than a linear SVM, which achieves 91% accuracy. This example illustrates a favorable accuracy–speed balance in the evaluated setting, alongside the broader computational improvement from structured landmarks.
icml-2016-computationally-efficient-nyst.tldr: Fast-transform landmarks reduce Nyström kernel-evaluation costs and substantially accelerate prediction in the reported experiment.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to measure the strength of a conditional relationship from one random variable to another. Its motivating distinction is between the relationship itself and how frequently different input values occur. For a known causal relationship, the desired strength measure depends on the effect’s conditional distribution given the cause, rather than the cause’s driving distribution.

The authors formulate axioms for such a measure and show that appropriately regularized Shannon capacity emerges as a natural choice. This provides a principled link between the desired properties of conditional dependence and a quantity from information theory. The causal application concerns assessing the strength of an already known relationship.

To estimate the quantity from observations, the paper introduces a nearest-neighbor estimator that keeps the neighbor count k fixed and demonstrates its consistency. An application to single-cell flow cytometry shows significantly reduced sample complexity. The work therefore combines a definition of what should be measured, a sample-based estimation procedure, and evidence that the estimator can reduce data requirements in the reported application.
icml-2016-conditional-dependence-via-sha.tldr: The paper motivates regularized Shannon capacity as a conditional-dependence measure and develops a consistent nearest-neighbor estimator.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the amount of experience needed to learn continuous control with deep reinforcement learning. Large neural representations can make model-free learning demanding in samples, restricting its usefulness for physical systems. The authors investigate two complementary changes intended to make learning more efficient.

The first is normalized advantage functions, or NAF, a continuous version of Q-learning. Its representation makes it possible to use Q-learning with experience replay on continuous tasks, providing an alternative to policy-gradient and actor–critic approaches. The authors report substantially improved performance on a set of simulated robotic control tasks.

The second technique uses learned models to accelerate model-free learning. In particular, local linear models that are repeatedly refitted prove especially effective in the reported study. The paper demonstrates substantially faster learning in domains where those models are applicable. The two contributions address efficiency through different routes: a representation suited to continuous Q-learning and model-based assistance that can further speed the learning process when the local modeling approach fits the domain.
icml-2016-continuous-deep-q-learning-wit.tldr: Normalized advantage functions enable continuous Q-learning, while repeatedly fitted local models further accelerate learning where applicable.

paragraphs: The paper introduces reinforcement-learning tasks in Minecraft to examine several difficulties together. Agents receive first-person visual observations, encounter delayed rewards, and must deal with high-dimensional input. They also need to use active perception appropriately, making the acquisition of useful observations part of successful behavior.

The tasks expose these challenges in a controllable way, allowing systematic comparisons between existing deep reinforcement-learning architectures and new architectures that use memory. Although the tasks are simple to describe, their combination of partial observability, visual complexity, delayed feedback, and perception requirements makes them difficult for the architectures studied.

The evaluation also tests performance in environments excluded from training. The authors report that their new memory-based architectures generalize better to these unseen environments than existing architectures. This finding concerns transfer within the evaluated tasks, alongside performance under the combined learning challenges. The contribution includes both a task collection for examining these capabilities and architectural evidence that memory-based designs can improve generalization in that setting.
icml-2016-control-of-memory-active-perce.tldr: Controlled Minecraft tasks show improved generalization from new memory-based reinforcement-learning architectures in the evaluated environments.

paragraphs: The paper studies representations for structured objects such as sequences, trees, and graphs. A conventional kernel pipeline first fixes how structures are compared and then trains a predictor. The authors identify two difficulties with that separation: scaling to millions of examples and using prediction-related information to shape the representation itself.

Their method, structure2vec, embeds latent-variable models into feature spaces and learns those spaces using discriminative information. Feature extraction proceeds through a sequence of function mappings resembling graphical-model inference, including mean field and belief propagation. This gives the representation a connection to structured probabilistic modeling while allowing it to adapt to the prediction task.

In applications involving millions of data points, the authors report twice the speed, models 10,000 times smaller, and state-of-the-art predictive performance. These are empirical findings for the studied applications. They support the central idea that representations inspired by latent-variable inference can be learned for prediction while also reducing the computational and storage burdens associated with large structured-data problems.
icml-2016-discriminative-embeddings-of-l.tldr: Structure2vec learns predictive representations of structured data through mappings inspired by latent-variable inference, with strong reported scalability.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation learns from a source distribution for use on a different target distribution. This paper questions whether making feature distributions look similar is enough when the relationship between features and labels also changes. It emphasizes that useful transferable components may change across domains, provided those changes can be identified.

The authors consider a causal setting in which the label Y causes the features X, and both the label distribution and the distribution of features conditional on labels change. Under appropriate assumptions, they seek components whose conditional distributions become invariant after suitable location and scale transformations. They simultaneously identify changes in the label distribution.

This approach makes transfer depend on understanding structured changes, rather than only suppressing differences between domains. A component can remain useful if its change can be accounted for through the proposed transformations. The paper provides theoretical analysis and evaluations on synthetic and real-world data supporting the method’s effectiveness within this setting. Its assumptions about causal direction and transformable conditional distributions are central to the formulation.
icml-2016-domain-adaptation-with-conditi.tldr: Under causal and transformation assumptions, the method transfers features by identifying conditional distribution changes alongside label-distribution shifts.

paragraphs: The paper develops faster iterative algorithms for canonical correlation analysis and the generalized eigenvector problem involving two symmetric matrices. These computations are important in data analysis and scientific computing, but large matrices make runtime a central concern. The authors focus on convergence guarantees together with favorable scaling in the input size.

They reduce canonical correlation analysis to computing the top k generalized eigenvectors. A general solution framework then needs only access to an approximate linear-system solver as a black box. This modular reduction makes solving linear systems the computational building block for the broader eigenvector and correlation problems.

Using accelerated gradient descent within the framework gives a runtime linear in the number of nonzero input entries and nearly linear in the number of requested components. The algorithms have global linear convergence, with dependencies on matrix condition numbers and eigenvalue gaps. Here, linear convergence describes geometric progress toward accuracy. The contribution establishes theoretical runtime and convergence improvements; the authors frame improved practical performance on large datasets as a hoped-for consequence.
icml-2016-efficient-algorithms-for-large.tldr: A framework based on approximate linear-system solves yields globally linearly convergent algorithms for generalized eigenvectors and canonical correlation analysis.

paragraphs: Nonconvex regularizers can improve estimation and prediction, but they make optimization harder. This paper addresses that computational difficulty for a large class of such regularizers. Its central move is to change where nonconvexity appears in the learning objective, making familiar optimization tools usable in the transformed formulation.

The authors transfer the nonconvex part of the regularizer into the loss. The remaining regularizer becomes convex, while the modified loss is guaranteed to remain smooth. This structure permits efficient algorithms originally designed for convex regularizers, including proximal methods and Frank–Wolfe methods. The overall objective still contains nonconvexity, now located in a part handled differently by those algorithms.

The paper proves that critical points of the transformed problem are also critical points of the original problem. That establishes a connection between the solutions reached under the two formulations without claiming global optimality. Extensive experiments across several nonconvex regularization problems report much faster performance than state-of-the-art nonconvex solvers, supporting the computational value of redistributing the difficult part of the objective.
icml-2016-efficient-learning-with-a-fami.tldr: Moving nonconvexity from the regularizer into a smooth loss enables efficient existing algorithms while preserving the stated critical-point relationship.

paragraphs: The paper improves algorithms for estimating a matrix’s top eigenvector. For an explicitly available matrix A, it computes an approximate top eigenvector of A transpose times A. The runtime depends on the number of nonzero entries, the dimension, stable rank, and relative eigenvalue gap, with logarithmic dependence on the inverse target error.

The main technique is a robust analysis of shift-and-invert preconditioning. It turns eigenvector computation into a sequence of approximately solved linear systems, which fast stochastic-gradient methods can handle. The analysis makes these approximate intermediate computations usable within the eigenvector algorithm and establishes the resulting runtime improvements.

The authors also study an online setting with independent, identically distributed samples from a distribution with a covariance matrix. Their refinement procedure assumes an initial vector already approximates the top eigenvector to a gap-dependent accuracy. Combining refinement with earlier initialization methods improves sample complexity and runtime under various distributional assumptions. Thus, the results cover both explicit matrices and sample-based estimation, while retaining the initialization and distribution conditions relevant to the online guarantees.
icml-2016-faster-eigenvector-computation.tldr: Robust shift-and-invert analysis accelerates top-eigenvector estimation by reducing it to approximate linear-system solves.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to average distance or kernel matrices describing relationships within different collections of points. The matrices can have different sizes, and their rows need not come with matching identities. This makes the averaging problem about reconciling relational structures, rather than simply averaging corresponding matrix entries.

The comparison uses a probabilistic mapping between rows of two matrices and measures how much that mapping distorts their internal relationships. Called the softassign criterion, it is a regularized form of Gromov–Wasserstein distance. The average, or barycenter, minimizes a weighted sum of these comparison values, making it a Fréchet mean under the chosen criterion.

The resulting optimization problem is nonconvex. The authors provide a fast iterative algorithm built from regularized optimal-transport tools and demonstrate applications to shape barycenters and prediction of molecular energy levels. These examples show how a common relational representation can support both averaging objects and prediction from their configurations, even when direct point-by-point alignment is unavailable.
icml-2016-gromov-wasserstein-averaging-o.tldr: A regularized Gromov–Wasserstein approach averages relational matrices without requiring equal sizes or predefined point correspondences.

paragraphs: The paper introduces interacting particle Markov chain Monte Carlo, or iPMCMC. Its central design is a pool of standard and conditional sequential Monte Carlo samplers that interact. As with related particle MCMC methods, the overall algorithm is a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler defined on an extended space.

The empirical question is whether interaction improves how effectively the sampler moves through its distribution. The authors report significant improvements in mixing rates compared with non-interacting particle MCMC samplers. They also compare against a single particle MCMC sampler given an equivalent computational and memory budget, reporting improved mixing in that comparison as well.

The budget-matched comparison matters because it evaluates the interacting design against an alternative with comparable resources. The reported benefit therefore goes beyond simply allocating more memory or computation in that experiment. The method is also suitable for distributed and multicore architectures, aligning its pool-based structure with parallel hardware. Together, these findings support interaction as a useful way to organize particle MCMC computation.
icml-2016-interacting-particle-markov-ch.tldr: Interacting particle MCMC combines multiple samplers and empirically improves mixing, including against a single sampler with matched resources.

paragraphs: The paper studies ranking when a large training dataset has low-quality relevance labels but a smaller validation dataset has high-quality labels. The objective is to use the abundant training data in a way that maximizes ranking quality on the more trustworthy validation set. This directly addresses the practical trade-off between label quality and acquisition cost.

The authors formulate two adjustments: changing the weights assigned to training instances and remapping their learning targets. Motivated by the Gauss–Markov theorem for linear regression, they develop a meta-gradient decision-tree framework that learns these weight and target functions through gradient-based hyperparameter optimization.

The higher-quality validation labels guide how the lower-quality training information is used. Weight learning changes the influence of examples, while target learning changes what the ranker is asked to predict from them. Experiments on a large real-world dataset report significant improvements when the framework is incorporated into state-of-the-art learning algorithms. The results support optimizing the treatment of imperfect labels as part of training the ranker.
icml-2016-metagradient-boosted-decision-.tldr: A meta-gradient tree framework uses high-quality validation labels to learn training weights and targets for ranking with noisy labels.

paragraphs: Imitation learning uses expert demonstrations to learn behavior when the underlying cost function is unknown. The paper addresses the computational burden of approaches that repeatedly solve planning or reinforcement-learning problems. Those intermediate problems can be difficult in large environments, and imperfect solutions can substantially damage imitation performance.

Within the apprenticeship-learning formalism, the authors develop model-free algorithms that work from sample trajectories supplied by an expert. They seek a parameterized stochastic policy that performs at least as well as the expert under an unknown cost function. Their approach uses policy gradients, putting optimization of the policy at the center of the learning procedure.

The algorithms are designed to scale to large continuous environments and have a guarantee of convergence to local minima. That guarantee describes the optimization destination and does not establish that every resulting policy reaches a global optimum. The contribution is an alternative route to apprenticeship learning that addresses the burden of repeated planning while retaining a stated local-convergence guarantee for its policy-gradient approach.
icml-2016-model-free-imitation-learning-.tldr: Model-free policy-gradient algorithms pursue apprenticeship learning in large continuous environments with guaranteed convergence to local minima.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Monte Carlo sampler that combines a modified Nosé–Poincaré Hamiltonian with Riemannian preconditioning. Its motivation joins several concerns: effective exploration, sampling from the canonical ensemble, and stability when stochastic gradients introduce noise. The authors seek dynamics that address these concerns within a Hamiltonian framework.

Their modified dynamics include corrections associated with the Riemannian manifold. The resulting symplectic algorithm samples from the canonical ensemble and uses structural information in the preconditioning matrices to traverse parameter space efficiently. This connects the geometry used to guide movement with the dynamics governing the sampling procedure.

For large-data settings, the authors also propose a stochastic version with additional Hamiltonian terms that correct for stochastic-gradient noise. This directly addresses the potentially destabilizing effect identified in their motivation. Experiments show strong performance on synthetic datasets and high-dimensional topic-modeling problems based on Poisson factor analysis. The contribution is both a geometry-aware sampling construction and a noise-corrected variant, with empirical support in the reported sampling applications.
icml-2016-robust-monte-carlo-sampling-us.tldr: A modified Hamiltonian sampler combines Riemannian geometry with canonical-ensemble sampling and a stochastic-gradient noise correction.

paragraphs: The paper studies anomaly detection for dynamic data streams using random cut forests. Its computational foundation is a robust random cut data structure that acts as a sketch, or compact synopsis, of the incoming data. The objective is to make anomaly detection compatible with a representation that can evolve as the stream changes.

The authors propose defining a nonparametric anomaly through its influence on the rest of the data. An unseen point is assessed by the externality it imposes: how its presence affects the other observations within this framework. This makes anomaly assessment relational, tying the unusualness of a point to its effect on the data already represented.

The paper shows how to update the sketch efficiently in a dynamic stream and demonstrates the algorithm’s viability on publicly available real data. These results support the feasibility of combining the proposed influence-based definition with a maintainable streaming representation. The stated empirical conclusion is practical viability, while the methodological contribution includes both the anomaly definition and the efficient data structure.
icml-2016-robust-random-cut-forest-based.tldr: Robust random cut forests detect streaming anomalies through a point’s influence on other data while maintaining an efficiently updated sketch.

paragraphs: The paper approaches tensor decomposition by extracting a collection of observable matrices from the tensor. It then applies an approximate joint Schur decomposition to those matrices. This creates a route from the original tensor problem to a coordinated matrix decomposition problem, with the matrices treated together.

The authors establish first-order perturbation bounds for the approach, describing its sensitivity to small changes. They also introduce an iterative Gauss–Newton algorithm for the joint matrix problem. Its objective is nonconvex, and optimization takes place over the manifold of orthogonal matrices, so the algorithm operates within a structured set of allowable transformations.

Under certain conditions, the algorithm is guaranteed to converge to a global optimum. Those conditions are part of the guarantee; the statement does not assert global convergence for every instance. Empirically, the algorithm is faster and at least as accurate and robust as state-of-the-art alternatives for this problem. The paper therefore combines a matrix-based reformulation, sensitivity analysis, conditional convergence theory, and favorable experimental comparisons.
icml-2016-tensor-decomposition-via-joint.tldr: Tensor decomposition is reduced to joint matrix Schur decomposition, with perturbation bounds and conditional global-convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Mixed-initiative classifier training lets a human choose examples to label or answer labeling requests chosen by the computer. The paper seeks a statistical learning explanation for the empirical success of combining those two sources of initiative. Its focus is label complexity: the labeling effort required by the training mechanism.

The analysis combines teaching dimension and active learning to study a simple mixed-initiative mechanism. It establishes an advantage over either computer-led active learning or human-led training alone. Within the analyzed setting, that advantage spans teaching abilities from optimal to completely unhelpful, making teacher quality an explicit part of the theoretical result.

The authors also improve training by educating human teachers, showing or explaining optimal teaching sets to them. Mechanical Turk experiments on two stylistic classification tasks illustrate this approach. The work therefore addresses both how to combine human and computer choices and how to help people choose more informative examples. Its theoretical result concerns the analyzed mechanism, while the human experiments illustrate the proposed teacher-education strategy.
icml-2016-the-label-complexity-of-mixed-.tldr: The paper establishes label-complexity advantages for a mixed human–computer training mechanism and explores teaching people to provide better examples.

paragraphs: The segmented infinite hidden Markov model addresses the problem of dividing a time series into relatively stable regimes. The key task is identifying when one regime gives way to another. Ordinary infinite hidden Markov models can struggle because they lack a mechanism for separating higher-level changes from lower-level dynamics within a regime.

Hierarchical hidden Markov models can represent these distinctions, but their inference procedures are more complex and expensive. The proposed segmented model introduces a hierarchical formulation while supporting a simple, efficient inference scheme. It is designed to retain the computational appeal of an infinite hidden Markov model while making it better suited to segmentation.

Across a variety of segmentation problems, the authors report that the segmented model outperforms the conventional infinite hidden Markov model. Its performance also matches or exceeds that of a more complicated hierarchical model. These findings support the proposed combination of hierarchy and efficient inference in the evaluated tasks, showing that additional segmentation structure can be useful without requiring the more elaborate inference of the compared hierarchical approach.
icml-2016-the-segmented-ihmm-a-simple-ef.tldr: The segmented iHMM adds hierarchy for time-series segmentation while retaining simple inference and achieving strong reported performance.

paragraphs: The paper explores neural-network training through alternating direction methods and Bregman iteration. Its motivation includes the difficulty of scaling conventional stochastic-gradient training across large clusters, as well as optimization problems associated with saturation, poor conditioning, and saddle points. The proposed method carries out training without gradient-descent steps.

The network-training objective is broken into a sequence of minimization substeps, each of which can be solved globally in closed form. This changes the computational work performed during training and avoids many difficulties that can slow gradient methods on highly nonconvex problems. Global solutions for individual substeps do not, by themselves, establish a global solution for the entire network.

The method also exhibits strong distributed scaling, with reported linear speedups even across thousands of cores. That result connects the optimization design to the paper’s large-scale computing motivation. The contribution is an alternative training procedure whose simple subproblem solutions support substantial parallel execution, with the stated scaling results showing its promise for training networks using large numbers of processing cores.
icml-2016-training-neural-networks-witho.tldr: An alternating-direction training method replaces gradient-descent steps with closed-form subproblem solves and reports linear speedups across thousands of cores.
